strengths: The paper investigates a novel and timely direction: using 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) as a compact, spatially adaptive visual substrate for vision-language alignment instead of dense RGB patches. It provides a first large-scale study of 2DGS in multimodal pretraining.

The systems contribution is concrete and useful: structured Gaussian initialization, luminance-aware L1 pruning, and batched CUDA kernels yield over 90x faster fitting and ~97% GPU utilization, making large-scale 2DGS dataset generation more feasible.

The parameter-efficient adaptation strategy—freezing the RGB-pretrained transformer backbone and training only ~7% of parameters via a splat-aware stem and Perceiver resampler—is practical and enables a controlled comparison against an RGB teacher under identical training conditions.

The paper is generally well organized, with clear motivation regarding edge-cloud bandwidth and token explosion, and helpful figures (e.g., Figs. 1, 5, and 6) that illustrate the pipeline and compression/accuracy trade-offs.

The empirical analysis provides useful observations: 2DGS encoders are robust across splat counts and moderate compression ratios (3–12x), and from-scratch training underperforms parameter-efficient adaptation, highlighting directions for future work.

The work opens a path toward transmission-efficient multimodal representations and identifies concrete open problems such as joint representation-alignment training, video/streaming extensions, and end-to-end edge-cloud evaluation.
weaknesses: The central motivation—edge-cloud transmission efficiency—is not experimentally validated. The paper reports compression ratios but does not measure actual bandwidth, energy consumption, latency, or on-device fitting cost, nor does it compare against standard image codecs (e.g., JPEG/WebP) or token-pruning baselines at matched accuracy/compression. The main practical claim therefore remains speculative.

The absolute performance is low and the gap to RGB is nontrivial: 2DGS encoders achieve 13–15% top-1 and 30–35% top-5 zero-shot ImageNet-1K accuracy, versus 18.5% and 40% for the RGB teacher, and both are far below standard CLIP baselines due to the limited 12.8M-sample training budget. The claim that 2DGS is a 'viable multimodal substrate' is weakly supported.

Evaluation breadth is limited to zero-shot ImageNet-1K classification on a single DataComp subset. No results are provided for retrieval, captioning, VQA, or other vision-language benchmarks, despite the paper's framing as vision-language alignment. Cross-dataset generalization is not tested.

Key components are not ablated for downstream alignment: structured initialization and luminance-aware pruning are evaluated only via image-fitting PSNR, not via zero-shot or retrieval accuracy. It is unclear whether these optimizations help or hurt semantic alignment, or whether pruning at 20–50% preserves downstream performance.

The method retains 98 or 196 output tokens—essentially the same as the RGB ViT-B-16 baseline—so the paper does not substantively address the token-explosion problem it identifies. No comparison is made to token-pruning methods (e.g., ToMe, PruMerge) under matched token counts.

Training only ~7% of parameters with a frozen backbone may underfit the 2DGS domain; the paper does not compare against fine-tuning more layers or full fine-tuning. The reported from-scratch experiments are insufficient to isolate the cause of the accuracy gap.

Reproducibility is limited: the optimized 2DGS pipeline is not yet open-sourced, and important details (exact CUDA kernel implementations, fitting hyperparameters, pruning thresholds, DataComp subset composition, tokenizer details) are missing. The compression ratio calculations also use float16 for all splat parameters without including metadata or codec overhead, and do not compare to a strong image codec baseline.

Some claims are overstated or insufficiently supported: 'semantically rich' and 'preserve information critical for downstream learning' are asserted but not measured; the connection between fitting PSNR and semantic alignment is not established; and the edge-cloud scenario assumes fitting can be done on edge devices without measuring its feasibility.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated direction: the paper reframes the compression problem by proposing 2D Gaussian Splatting as an inherently compact, spatially adaptive visual substrate for vision-language alignment, rather than treating compression as post-hoc token pruning. The motivation is concretely grounded in edge-cloud energy figures (0.1-0.2 kWh/GB uplink) and token-explosion statistics (576-2880 tokens/image in LLaVA variants).

Solid, verifiable systems contribution: batched CUDA kernels with batch-aware memory layout, synchronization threads, and shared-memory caching yield up to ~90x faster 2DGS fitting and ~97% GPU utilization (Fig. 2), and structured initialization achieves 33.07 PSNR vs 21.09 for random initialization at 4900 Gaussians (Fig. 3) - both are concrete and reproducible improvements that make large-scale GS fitting feasible.

Parameter-efficient adaptation recipe is sensible: freezing the RGB ViT-B-16 backbone and training only ~7% of parameters through a splat-aware stem (Fourier positional encoding, log-scaled covariance, gated sigmoid layer, z-score normalization) and a Perceiver Resampler is a reasonable design that isolates the effect of the representation.

Honest and transparent reporting: the paper explicitly states the 3-5 point accuracy gap to RGB encoders, reports the failure of from-scratch training (Fig. 7), and flags omitted codec-side quantization and other limitations, which strengthens credibility.

Empirical robustness trends are informative: results remain stable across splat counts (400-3136) and compression ratios (3-12x), and the 196-token configuration consistently beats the 98-token variant (Fig. 6), suggesting the resampler captures meaningful information even at high compression.
weaknesses: The RGB baseline is unusually weak and hard to interpret: a CLIP ViT-B-16 trained on a 12.8M DataComp subset with reduced width (38M) reaches only 18.5% top-1 on ImageNet-1K, whereas standard CLIP ViT-B/16 reaches ~68%. Because both the teacher and the 2DGS student are far outside the standard training regime, the central 13-15% vs 18.5% comparison is difficult to generalize and provides no absolute reference for whether 2DGS is competitive.

The paper's core transmission-efficiency claim is not supported by the right baselines. There is no matched-bitrate comparison against JPEG/WebP + CLIP, and no comparison against the alternative representations the paper explicitly positions itself against: token-pruning methods (ToMe, VisionZip, PruMerge) or INR-based substrates (WIRE, I-NGP). The reported '3-23.5x compression' is only relative to raw pixels; against typical JPEG rates (often ~10-20x at near-negligible quality loss) the advantage is not established, and the compression ratio definition (bits vs float16 parameters) is unclear.

Evaluation is narrow relative to the claims: only zero-shot ImageNet-1K classification on a single DataComp subset is reported. Claims about 'vision-language alignment' and 'multimodal systems' are not tested on retrieval, VQA, captioning, or any downstream multimodal task, leaving the headline framing only partially evidenced.

The methodological components are largely standard (Fourier positional encoding, Perceiver Resampler, gated linear layers, L1 pruning, grid-based initialization); the contribution is primarily integration and engineering rather than a fundamentally new method, which limits the technical novelty beyond the systems layer.

Reproducibility and maturity concerns: results are based on a single training run without variance or error bars, the codebase is promised rather than released ('will soon be open-sourced'), and the manuscript repeatedly describes results as 'preliminary,' which weakens confidence in the robustness of the conclusions.

strengths: The problem framing is relevant and well articulated: edge-to-cloud bandwidth/energy cost of dense RGB transfer and the token explosion in ViT-based VLMs are real inefficiencies, and the paper sensibly connects them to a representation-level question rather than another post-hoc token-pruning heuristic.

The systems contribution is concrete and potentially useful to the 2DGS community: batched CUDA kernels with batch-aware memory layout, added synchronization, and shared-memory caching are described in enough detail to be re-implementable, and the reported fitting speedups (33.5x-90.3x over the LIG baseline) and ~97% GPU utilization are meaningful engineering results.

Structured initialization and the L1/luminance-aware adaptive pruning are simple, sensible, and empirically justified for the fitting task (Fig. 3: 33.07 vs 21.09 PSNR at 4900 Gaussians; 25.75 vs 18.48 at 400), and the pruning visualizations in Fig. 4 make the trade-off between splat count and perceptual quality legible.

The parameter-efficient adaptation recipe (frozen RGB ViT backbone, trainable GS stem + Perceiver resampler, ~7% of parameters) is a reasonable and clearly documented strategy, and the negative result on training 2DGS encoders from scratch (Fig. 7) is reported honestly rather than hidden.

The manuscript is generally clear, the related work is broad, and the authors are upfront about the accuracy gap and about what remains future work (codec-side quantization, end-to-end edge-cloud energy measurement).
weaknesses: The headline efficiency claim is measured against the wrong baseline. All compression ratios (3x-23.5x) are computed relative to raw, uncompressed RGB pixels (Fig. 6 axis is explicitly 'Compression Ratio (vs. pixel domain)'), even though the introduction motivates the problem by arguing that even JPEG-compressed RGB 'remains bandwidth-intensive.' No comparison against JPEG/WebP at matched bitrate is provided, so the practical advantage over the status quo is unknown. Concretely, 400 Gaussians x 8 params x 2 bytes = 6.4 KB versus 150 KB raw RGB gives 23.5x, but a 224x224 JPEG at reasonable quality is already roughly 10-15 KB; the claimed advantage over a realistic codec is therefore small or absent, and this is never tested.

The central 'effectiveness' claim is not supported by the evidence. The best 2DGS models reach 13-15% zero-shot ImageNet-1K top-1 against an RGB teacher at 18.5% top-1 / 40% top-5. In absolute terms both numbers are far below even weak CLIP baselines (ViT-B/16 CLIP is ~68% zero-shot ImageNet), indicating a very small-scale regime (12.8M DataComp subset, 38M-width encoder, 32 epochs). Whether the 3-5 point gap persists, widens, or closes at realistic scale is entirely unknown, yet the abstract and conclusion make forward-looking claims about 2DGS as a 'viable multimodal substrate' on the basis of this single, unusually weak operating point.

Evaluation breadth is far too narrow for the claims. Despite pages of related work on multimodal tasks and token reduction, the only downstream metric is zero-shot ImageNet-1K classification. There is no retrieval, VQA, captioning, or grounding result, and no comparison against the token-pruning/sparsification methods (ToMe, FastV, SparseVLM, PruMerge, VisionZip) that the paper itself frames as the competing paradigm. A reader cannot tell whether 2DGS inputs preserve 'semantic and structural content' better than a pruned RGB pipeline at comparable token counts - the comparison that would actually test the thesis.

The energy and bandwidth motivation is never validated. The paper's premise is transmission efficiency for edge-cloud learning, but no end-to-end measurement (bits on the wire, latency, energy) is reported, and the on-device cost of fitting Gaussians is not accounted for. Fitting requires iterative forward/backward passes through a differentiable renderer; even at the claimed 90x speedup this is non-trivial compute on an edge device, and it is not included in any cost model. The authors explicitly defer this to future work, which leaves the motivating argument unsubstantiated.

Novelty of the modeling contribution is modest and partially anticipated. Representing images as Gaussians for vision tasks already exists (GViT, GaussianToken), and the proposed 'GS stem' is a composition of standard parts - Fourier positional encoding, log-scaled covariance, z-score normalization, a gated sigmoid layer, and a Perceiver resampler. No ablation isolates the contribution of these components to downstream accuracy; the only ablation (Fig. 3) concerns reconstruction PSNR from initialization, not alignment quality.

The 'over 90x faster fitting' claim in the abstract and conclusion is the maximum of a range that in Fig. 2 actually spans 33.5x-90.3x depending on batch size and splat count. Reporting only the best case overstates the typical speedup.

The results depend heavily on RGB-pretrained priors, which undercuts the 'native substrate' narrative: training from scratch fails (Fig. 7), so the reported alignment is largely inherited from the frozen RGB backbone, and the pipeline still requires a full RGB image to fit the Gaussians in the first place. The paper does not discuss whether the edge device must transmit the fitted Gaussians (requiring local optimization) or the raw image (defeating the purpose).

Several presentation issues: the title contains '2D Gaussian Splitting' rather than 'Splatting'; the abstract phrase '~97% GPU utilization compared to prior implementations' is grammatically garbled; the two plots in Fig. 6 have confusing axes (compression ratio derived from splat count, plotted against accuracy) and neither plot shows the RGB reference line for direct comparison; and the code is promised 'soon' rather than released, limiting reproducibility of the systems claims.

strengths: First large-scale exploration of 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) as a visual representation for vision-language alignment, using 12.8M DataComp images and evaluating on 38 CLIP benchmark datasets.
Provides a thorough empirical study with multiple Gaussian point budgets (400, 900, 1600, 3136), two-stage training, and extensive ablations in the appendix.

Introduces practical systems and algorithmic optimizations for scalable 2DGS fitting, including structured initialization, luminance-aware pruning, and batched CUDA kernels with reported speedups and open-source plans.
Demonstrates competitive relative accuracy (roughly 90–98% of the RGB baseline) under substantial input compression and faster data loading, suggesting potential for compact visual representations.
Writing is generally clear, and the appendix provides detailed architecture, hyperparameters, and training recipes, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core representation is not self-sufficient: the GS encoder is initialized and distilled from a frozen RGB ViT teacher, and training from scratch performs poorly (Fig. 21). This makes the method fundamentally upper-bounded by RGB-pretrained features and weakens the claim that 2DGS is a viable alternative multimodal substrate.

The compression and efficiency comparisons are unfair because they use uncompressed RGB as the baseline rather than standard image codecs (e.g., JPEG/WebP/AVIF). The reported 3–23.5x compression and 6.7–13x data loading speedups may not hold against realistic JPEG-compressed inputs, undermining the edge-cloud transmission motivation.

There is a significant inconsistency in the reported preprocessing cost: Table 4 states that fitting the entire 12.8M dataset takes 25.6–53.1 GPU hours, but the profiling in Table 3 implies roughly 200–280 GPU hours for the 3136–4000 point configurations. This factor of ~4–5 discrepancy suggests a technical error or misinterpretation that affects scalability claims.

The adaptive pruning contribution is not integrated into the main vision-language pipeline; the main CLIP results use non-pruned FP16 Gaussian parameters. Thus the pruning is only evaluated for fitting efficiency, not for final compression or downstream accuracy.

The method suffers severe performance drops on some benchmark datasets, e.g., diabetic retinopathy drops from 38.33 (RGB) to 3.09 (GS-3136). The paper acknowledges distribution shift but does not analyze or mitigate this loss of critical information.

Evaluation is limited to zero-shot classification; no retrieval or other vision-language tasks are reported. The model scale is also limited to a reduced-width ViT-B/16 (Small) and 12.8M images, without validation on larger-scale models or datasets.

Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to prior work such as GViT and GaussianToken; the main architectural addition is a Perceiver-based stem on top of a frozen RGB ViT, not a GS-native architecture that could exploit the representation's unique properties.

strengths: Addresses a timely and well-motivated problem (edge–cloud transmission cost and token explosion) with a genuinely different framing: treating the visual substrate itself as the design variable rather than compressing pixels or pruning tokens post hoc. The question 'are patch-based encoders the right substrate for multimodal alignment?' is a legitimate research contribution independent of any single benchmark number.

The systems/algorithmic contribution is concrete and verifiable: batch-aware memory layout, added synchronization, expanded shared memory, grid-based structured initialization, and L1 + luminance-threshold pruning yield up to 90x faster fitting and ~97% kernel fraction of active GPU time (Nsight-profiled in Table 3), enabling offline fitting of the full 12.8M-image DataComp set in only 25.6-53.1 GPU hours (Table 4). This is a useful, reusable artifact for the community.

Evaluation breadth is substantial: 38 CLIP-benchmark datasets, four Gaussian budgets (400/900/1600/3136) crossed with two token counts (98/196), plus a rich appendix with ablations over distillation strategy, distillation loss (cosine vs. InfoNCE vs. similarity-preserving), normalization scheme, GS-stem architecture (Perceiver vs. conv vs. grid vs. point transformer), logit-scale init, text-freezing, and learning rate. The token-reduction baseline for RGB is also examined rather than assumed.

The paper is candid about limitations in Sec. 6 and the case studies: training GS encoders from scratch converges poorly (Fig. 21), performance is upper-bounded by the RGB teacher, GS encoders are more sensitive to distribution shift, and fitting remains non-trivial. This honesty makes the claims easier to calibrate and the negative results (Sec. 11.6) are themselves informative.

Reproducibility is reasonably well supported: the work builds on an open 2DGS codebase, all hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, epochs, schedule, thresholds) are reported, the encoder forward pass is given as pseudocode (Alg. 1), and the authors commit to open-sourcing preprocessing, CUDA kernels, and the CLIP pipeline.
weaknesses: The headline 'compression' claim is measured only against uncompressed RGB (Table 1 divides by 224x224x3 bytes). No comparison is made to JPEG/WebP or to simple spatial downsampling, which are the practically relevant transmission baselines. A quality-75 JPEG of a 224x224 image is roughly an order of magnitude smaller than the reported 3.00x for GS-3136, and a standard CLIP ViT on such JPEGs would retain near-full accuracy - potentially dominating the proposed substrate on the paper's own motivating axis. The compression argument is therefore not established against a strong baseline, and since the pipeline uses non-pruned FP16 splats (as the authors acknowledge), the reported ratios are a lower bound rather than a competitive operating point.

There is a tension between the edge-cloud motivation and the method's encoder-side cost. Producing splats requires an iterative GPU optimization (2000 iterations/image, ~7-15 ms/image in heavily batched settings) plus a frozen RGB teacher for the distillation stage. The paper never analyzes how a resource-constrained edge device would generate the representation, nor its encode-time energy, which is the very quantity the motivation section quantifies (0.1-0.2 kWh/GB uplink).

Retention is 90-98% of RGB *relative* accuracy, i.e., a 2-10% relative drop, and all GS encoders are distilled from an RGB-pretrained teacher, so the representation is not shown to be independently competitive. Claims such as '19 datasets are best solved by one of the GS variants' and 'often outperform the RGB baseline' are not supported by significance testing and are confounded by the fact that GS variants contribute more entries per dataset (four budgets x two token counts), mechanically inflating the chance of holding the best score.

The token-efficiency comparison is partly an artifact of the baseline construction. The 98-token RGB reference is formed by averaging adjacent patch embeddings after positional encoding, which the authors themselves note is 'a practical proxy' rather than a fair comparison; their own 5-epoch finetuned variant raises the RGB-98 relative accuracy from 0.87 to 0.95 (Table 7), substantially closing the gap that the GS pipeline is credited with. The remaining token-count advantage is thus not cleanly attributable to the GS substrate.

Generality is limited to a single backbone scale (a 38M-parameter width-reduced ViT-B/16), a single training corpus (12.8M DataComp pairs, modest by current CLIP standards), and no scaling study. The 'first large-scale' framing would be stronger with at least one larger backbone or data scale. Relatedly, no head-to-head comparison is provided against other compact substrates under identical training (e.g., INR/WIRE encodings or GaussianToken-style tokenizers), so the claim that 2DGS is a superior substrate relative to alternatives is not directly tested.

Presentation imprecision in the main claims: the abstract's '~97% GPU utilization' actually refers to the kernel fraction of *active* GPU time from Nsight (Table 3), not SM utilization; the main-text results are shown as bar plots (Fig. 6) with the quantitative table relegated to the appendix, which makes the central accuracy claim harder to verify from the main paper alone.

strengths: The problem framing is genuinely interesting and well-motivated: exploring 2D Gaussian Splatting as an inherently compact visual substrate for vision–language alignment, motivated by edge–cloud bandwidth costs and token explosion, is a fresh and reasonable research question worth asking.

The systems/engineering contribution is non-trivial and potentially useful to the community: batched CUDA kernels for 2DGS fitting (Fig. 2, Table 3) enable fitting a 12.8M-image dataset offline, with concrete throughput profiling (Nsight) and reported batch-size/throughput tradeoffs.

The ablation suite in the appendix is unusually thorough (structured vs. random init, pruning sweeps, distillation loss variants, GS-stem architectures, point-transformer study, normalization, hyperparameter sensitivity), and the authors are relatively candid about several limitations in Sec. 6 and 11.6 (e.g., scratch training converging poorly, distribution-shift sensitivity).

Structured initialization (grid positions, isotropic covariance, mean color) and luminance-aware pruning are sensible, well-visualized heuristics (Figs. 3, 4, 5, 7, 8) that clearly improve convergence over random init in the 2D setting.
weaknesses: The central claim that 2DGS is a 'semantically powerful' and 'viable multimodal substrate' is largely circular. The GS encoder inherits an RGB-pretrained ViT-B/16 backbone and is trained by distilling the frozen RGB teacher's CLS embeddings (Sec. 5.2). Therefore 'GS retains 90–98% of RGB accuracy' mostly measures how well distillation transfers RGB semantics into a GS-input model, not the intrinsic semantic content of Gaussian splats. The authors themselves concede this in Sec. 11.6 ('its achievable zero-shot performance is similarly bounded by the representational limits of the underlying pixel-domain ViT'), but the abstract and title do not reflect this and overclaim accordingly.

The compression claim is misleading and, for the stated edge–cloud motivation, arguably invalid. Compression ratio is computed only against *uncompressed* RGB (224×224×3×1 byte). No comparison to JPEG is provided despite the paper explicitly citing JPEG and admitting (Sec. 6) that 2DGS is not yet more compressed than JPEG. At 1600 points × 8 params × 2 bytes = 25.6 KB per image, the GS representation is likely *larger* than a comparable-quality JPEG, so the '3–23.5× compression' framing collapses under the most natural baseline. Additionally, obtaining the GS representation requires running a GPU fitting pipeline (seconds per batch) on the RGB image — meaning either the edge device needs a GPU and RGB input, or RGB must be transmitted to the cloud anyway. The headline efficiency benefit is therefore never empirically validated.

Baselines are not matched and the key comparison is buried. The main table (Table 1) compares GS variants against a reduced-width ViT-B/16 (dim 512) using a naive 98-token averaging baseline that scores only 0.87 relative. Table 7 in the appendix shows that a properly fine-tuned 98-token RGB baseline reaches 20.56 average absolute accuracy — *higher* than GS-1600 (20.31) and GS-3136 (20.39). The claim that 'GS often matches or even outperforms the RGB baseline' (Sec. 6) therefore largely disappears when the RGB baseline is given a fair recipe, which is disclosed only in the appendix.

No comparison to any of the post-hoc token-reduction methods that the related work section extensively criticizes (ToMe, PruMerge, VisionZip, SparseVLM, etc.), nor to learned compact-token approaches (VQ-VAE, the cited GaussianToken). The paper's core positioning ('beyond post-hoc pruning toward inherently compact representations') is never empirically substantiated against these alternatives, even though such comparisons would be straightforward on the same backbone.

Headline system claims are thin and over-stated. The '90× faster fitting and ~97% GPU utilization' numbers in the abstract derive from a single baseline implementation (Zhu et al. [41]) and, per Fig. 2, only at large batch sizes; the speedup is essentially batching, not a novel algorithmic result. The 97% utilization is asserted without substantive profiling evidence or ablation of what specifically drives it.

Overall accuracy levels (absolute mean ~20–22% over 38 datasets) are very low, and the aggregation via 'relative accuracy' (mean of per-dataset ratios) can obscure where the model fails. The paper acknowledges that GS 'underperforms more substantially' on some datasets tied to distribution shift but does not analyze these failures, which would be the most informative evidence about the limits of the representation.

Novelty is limited relative to the strength of the claims. Structured initialization, luminance pruning, and RGB→GS distillation are all natural, incremental engineering choices; the 'first large-scale study' framing is a claim of priority rather than a technical contribution. Code is promised but not available, and CUDA-kernel details are insufficiently specified for reproduction.
